body:
What is motion?

An object is said to be in motion when its position changes with time relative to a chosen reference point. A person walking along a road, a moving bicycle and a ball rolling across a field are familiar examples.

An object is at rest when its position does not change with time relative to the chosen reference point. Rest and motion are therefore described with respect to an observer or reference point.

Why is a reference point necessary?

Consider a passenger sitting in a moving bus. The passenger is at rest relative to the seat because the distance and direction between the passenger and the seat remain unchanged. However, a person standing beside the road sees the passenger moving along with the bus.

Neither observation is incorrect. The observers are using different reference points. Similarly, roadside trees appear to move backwards to a passenger looking out of a moving bus, although the trees remain stationary relative to the road.

A reference point is a point or object chosen to describe the position and motion of another object. The selected starting point for measuring position is often called the origin.

Position and direction

Suppose a railway station is selected as the origin. A school located 2 km east of the station can be described by both its distance and direction from that origin. On a straight line, one direction may be chosen as positive and the opposite direction as negative. For example, east may be positive and west negative.

This sign convention becomes important when calculating displacement, velocity and acceleration. Once a positive direction has been selected for a numerical problem, it should be used consistently.

Common types of motion

  • Rectilinear motion: Motion along a straight line, such as a vehicle travelling along a straight road.
  • Circular motion: Motion along a circular path, such as a point on a rotating fan blade.
  • Periodic motion: Motion that repeats after equal intervals of time, such as the oscillations of a simple pendulum.

Some objects show more than one type of motion simultaneously. For example, a wheel rolling along a straight road rotates about its axle while the wheel as a whole moves forward.

Prelims focus

  • Motion is a change in position with time relative to a reference point.
  • An object can be at rest for one observer and moving for another.
  • Rectilinear motion follows a straight-line path.
  • Circular motion follows a circular path.
  • Trap: Motion cannot be described completely without identifying the reference point or frame of observation.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 10, 'Motion and Measurement of Distances', pp. 102–105, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', pp. 98–99, 2018–19 print.]

title: Understanding Motion: Rest, Reference Points and Types of Motion

body:
Distance travelled

Distance is the total length of the actual path covered by an object during its motion. It does not indicate direction. If a person walks 60 m east and then 20 m west, the total distance travelled is 80 m.

Distance is a scalar quantity, which means that it is specified by magnitude alone. Its SI unit is the metre (m). The distance travelled during an interval cannot be negative because path length is non-negative.

Displacement

Displacement describes the change from an object's initial position to its final position. It is a vector quantity, meaning that both magnitude and direction are important.

For motion along a straight line, displacement is calculated by subtracting the initial position from the final position:

$$\Delta x=x_f-x_i$$

Here, \(x_i\) is the initial position and \(x_f\) is the final position. A positive or negative sign indicates direction according to the chosen convention.

Worked example: A journey with a change in direction

A person starts at position 0 m, walks 60 m east and then returns 20 m west. Choose east as positive.

  • Initial position = 0 m.
  • Position after walking east = +60 m.
  • Final position after returning = +40 m.
  • Total distance = 60 m + 20 m = 80 m.
  • Displacement = +40 m − 0 m = 40 m east.

The distance includes both parts of the journey, whereas the displacement depends only on the starting and finishing positions.

Important differences

PropertyDistanceDisplacement
MeaningTotal path lengthChange in position
TypeScalarVector
Depends onActual routeInitial and final positions
DirectionNot requiredRequired
SI unitMetre (m)Metre (m)

When are distance and displacement equal?

The magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance travelled:

$$|\Delta x|\leq \text{distance travelled}$$

They are equal when the object travels along a straight path without reversing direction. If the object changes direction or follows a longer route, the distance is greater than the magnitude of displacement.

For a complete round trip that ends at the starting point, displacement is zero even though distance travelled may be considerable. A runner completing 1 full lap of a 400 m track travels 400 m but has zero displacement for the complete lap.

Distance and the odometer

An automobile's odometer records the distance travelled by the vehicle. It does not directly show displacement because it does not specify the final position relative to the starting point.

Prelims focus

  • Distance is a scalar; displacement is a vector.
  • Both have the SI unit metre.
  • The magnitude of displacement is less than or equal to distance travelled.
  • A round trip may have zero displacement and non-zero distance.
  • An odometer measures distance travelled.
  • Trap: Displacement is not the total distance divided by the number of directions travelled.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', sections 8.1.1 and 8.2, pp. 98–102, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 13, 'Motion and Time', section 13.4, pp. 149–151, 2018–19 print.]

pictures.alt: From O, travel 60 m east to A, then 20 m west to B: distance is 80 m, while displacement is 40 m east.
pictures.caption: The actual path is 80 m, but the final position is only 40 m east of the starting point.

title: Distance and Displacement: Path Length Versus Change in Position

body:
Speed is distance covered per unit time

Speed measures how quickly an object covers distance. It is calculated by dividing the distance travelled by the time taken.

$$\text{Average speed}=\frac{\text{Total distance travelled}}{\text{Total time taken}}$$

Speed is a scalar quantity. Its SI unit is metre per second (m/s). Kilometre per hour (km/h) is also commonly used for vehicles.

If a cyclist covers 60 m in 10 s, the average speed is \(60/10=6\) m/s. If another cyclist covers the same 60 m in 15 s, the average speed is \(60/15=4\) m/s. Thus, covering the same distance in less time gives a higher average speed.

Velocity includes direction

Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with time. Unlike speed, it includes direction and is therefore a vector quantity.

$$\text{Average velocity}=\frac{\text{Displacement}}{\text{Total time taken}}$$

For example, if a person moves 40 m east in 10 s along a straight path without turning, the average velocity is 4 m/s east. The numerical value is equal to the average speed because the person has travelled along a straight path in one direction.

Average speed and average velocity can differ

Suppose a swimmer travels 50 m from one end of a straight swimming pool to the other end and then returns to the starting point. The entire journey takes 40 s.

  • Total distance = 50 m + 50 m = 100 m.
  • Total displacement = 0 m because the starting and final positions coincide.
  • Average speed = 100/40 = 2.5 m/s.
  • Average velocity = 0/40 = 0 m/s.

The swimmer was moving throughout the journey but has zero average velocity over the complete round trip.

Average velocity is determined by net displacement, not total distance. A moving object can therefore have zero average velocity without having zero average speed.

Uniform speed and uniform velocity

An object has uniform speed when it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time. It has uniform velocity only when both its speed and direction remain constant.

A vehicle moving along a straight road at a constant speed has uniform velocity. A cyclist moving around a circular track at constant speed does not have uniform velocity because the direction of motion changes continuously.

Speedometer and unit conversion

A vehicle's speedometer indicates its speed at a particular time, whereas the odometer records accumulated distance.

To convert speed from km/h to m/s, multiply by \(\frac{5}{18}\). To convert from m/s to km/h, multiply by \(\frac{18}{5}\).

$$36\ \text{km/h}=36\times\frac{5}{18}=10\ \text{m/s}$$

Comparison at a glance

PropertySpeedVelocity
Based onDistanceDisplacement
TypeScalarVector
DirectionNot requiredRequired
SI unitm/sm/s

Prelims focus

  • Average speed = total distance divided by total time.
  • Average velocity = displacement divided by total time.
  • Uniform velocity requires constant speed and constant direction.
  • 36 km/h = 10 m/s.
  • Trap: Constant speed does not necessarily mean constant velocity.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 13, 'Motion and Time', sections 13.1, 13.2 and 13.4, pp. 143–151, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', section 8.2, pp. 100–102, 2018–19 print.]

pictures.alt: Both cyclists cover 60 m: A takes 10 s at 6 m/s, while B takes 15 s at 4 m/s; the shorter time means greater average speed.
pictures.caption: For the same distance, the cyclist taking less time has the greater average speed.

title: Speed and Velocity: Measuring How Fast an Object Moves

body:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity

When the velocity of an object changes with time, the object is said to be accelerating. Acceleration may result from an increase in speed, a decrease in speed or a change in direction.

For straight-line motion, average acceleration is:

$$a=\frac{v-u}{t}$$

Here, \(u\) is initial velocity, \(v\) is final velocity and \(t\) is the elapsed time. The SI unit of acceleration is m/s2.

Positive and negative acceleration

Choose the forward direction as positive. If a vehicle's velocity increases from +2 m/s to +10 m/s in 4 s, its acceleration is:

$$a=\frac{10-2}{4}=+2\ \text{m/s}^2$$

If the same vehicle slows from +10 m/s to +2 m/s in 4 s, its acceleration is:

$$a=\frac{2-10}{4}=-2\ \text{m/s}^2$$

When acceleration acts opposite to velocity, the object's speed decreases. This is called deceleration or retardation.

A negative acceleration does not always mean that an object is slowing down. The negative sign indicates direction. If both velocity and acceleration are negative, the object's speed can increase.

Uniform and non-uniform acceleration

Uniform acceleration occurs when velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time. Non-uniform acceleration occurs when the rate of change of velocity is not constant.

For example, an object starting from rest and accelerating uniformly at 2 m/s2 travels 4 m in the first 2 s and another 12 m in the next 2 s. It covers more distance during the second interval because it is moving faster.

Equations of uniformly accelerated motion

For motion along a straight line with constant acceleration, 3 equations connect initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time and displacement.

First equation: Velocity–time relation

$$v=u+at$$

Second equation: Displacement–time relation

$$s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^2$$

Third equation: Velocity–displacement relation

$$v^2=u^2+2as$$

In these equations, \(s\) represents the signed displacement along the selected straight-line axis. When the object moves only in the positive direction without turning back, displacement also equals distance travelled.

Worked example: Vehicle starting from rest

A vehicle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s2 for 5 s.

Given: \(u=0\), \(a=2\) m/s2 and \(t=5\) s.

Final velocity:

$$v=0+(2\times5)=10\ \text{m/s}$$

Distance travelled:

$$s=0+\frac{1}{2}\times2\times5^2=25\ \text{m}$$

The final velocity is 10 m/s and the distance travelled is 25 m.

Worked example: Braking to rest

A vehicle moving at 10 m/s slows uniformly at 2 m/s2 and comes to rest. Taking forward as positive, \(a=-2\) m/s2.

Using \(v=u+at\):

$$0=10-2t\quad\Rightarrow\quad t=5\ \text{s}$$

Using \(s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^2\):

$$s=10\times5+\frac{1}{2}(-2)\times5^2=25\ \text{m}$$

The vehicle takes 5 s to stop and travels 25 m during braking under the stated constant-acceleration assumption.

Prelims focus

  • Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time.
  • The SI unit of acceleration is m/s2.
  • Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
  • The 3 standard equations apply to uniformly accelerated straight-line motion.
  • For an object starting from rest, initial velocity \(u=0\).
  • Trap: The equations do not directly give total path length after a reversal unless the separate parts of the motion are considered.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', sections 8.3 and 8.5, pp. 102–109, 2018–19 print.]

title: Acceleration and the Three Equations of Motion
